clue.text: Having the gall to serve absinthe

definitions.meaning: gall here is bitterness of spirit
the green spirit is flavoured with this bitter plant and the plant's name is used for the drink

explanation.surface: Someone has the cheek to pour out a glass of absinthe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Having the' and 'to serve' just join the two senses; 'gall' reads as cheek but means bitterness.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses are listed: the bitter herb stands for bitterness itself, and also names the spirit distilled with it.

clue.text: Mineral offered in old china

parts.note: china is rhyming slang (china plate = mate) for a friend or pal

explanation.surface: A gemstone is put on sale inside an antique porcelain dish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'china' looks like porcelain, but in Cockney rhyming slang 'china plate' means mate.
explanation.definitionFit: This iridescent silica gemstone is a mineraloid, loosely classed as a mineral.

clue.text: Assemble relay of workers as temporary measure

parts.note: to assemble something is to make it
a shift is a group of workers who take over in turn

explanation.surface: Management puts together a rota of workers as a stopgap.
explanation.definitionFit: A stopgap arrangement used until something better is available is a classic example of this.

clue.text: Supported by customs duties

parts.note: a thing supported by another sits on it
customs are habits or usages, so uses

explanation.surface: A government is funded by import tariffs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'customs duties' reads as one tax phrase; split it, and 'customs' is wordplay while 'duties' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Burdens or responsibilities are duties, the plural of the Latin-derived word for a burden.

clue.text: Closely follow steps leading to gate

parts.note: a dance is a series of steps
the gate at a sports match is the number attending

explanation.surface: Someone shadows a person's footsteps as they head towards the gate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gate' looks like a doorway; in British sport it is the crowd figure at a match.
explanation.definitionFit: This idiom means to wait on someone obsequiously, following them about at every turn.

clue.text: Make a point of not including bar

definitions.text: Make a point of not including
definitions.meaning: as a verb it means to leave something out deliberately, to exclude
as a preposition bar means 'apart from', as in 'all bar one'

explanation.surface: Someone deliberately leaves out the pub from the plan.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means to exclude, and the preposition means 'apart from', exactly as bar does in 'all bar one'.

clue.text: Going to ground with a hearing device, possibly

parts.note: to give someone a hearing is to lend them an ear
a device, a gadget, is a thing

explanation.surface: A fox heads for its den carrying something like a hearing aid.
explanation.walkthrough: 'possibly' flags that the definition and split are playful: read as two words the answer is a gadget for the ear.
explanation.definitionFit: Electrically, connecting a circuit to the ground is this; a fox driven into its hole is also said to be doing it.

clue.text: Banter heard at first in greasy spoon

indicators.note: the letter from heard goes inside the word for the café

parts.note: a greasy spoon is a cheap British café, a caff in slang

indicators.note: at first asks for the opening letter of heard

explanation.surface: Joking is overheard first at a cheap café.
explanation.walkthrough: A greasy spoon is a British slang name for a cheap café, colloquially a caff.
explanation.definitionFit: Light-hearted teasing or joking talk is a long-standing British synonym for banter.

clue.text: Coped with rural version of how to do business

indicators.note: a version of the words is a rearranged form of them

explanation.surface: Someone managed with a countryside way of doing things.
explanation.walkthrough: 'version of' reshuffles COPED and RURAL together.
explanation.definitionFit: Rules about the manner of conducting business are this kind of matter, as opposed to substantive ones.

clue.text: Where, oddly enough, one may put something on ice

definitions.text: Where, oddly enough, one may put something on ice

parts.words: Where, oddly enough, one may put something on ice
parts.note: putting a plan on ice means postponing it, and the place for postponed matters is oddly a hot ring at the rear of a cooker

explanation.surface: A cook wonders where to set down something to keep it chilled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'oddly enough' admits the joke: a place of heat is where things are kept 'on ice', meaning postponed.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiomatically, a matter shelved for later is put on this rear cooker ring, as if left to simmer unattended.

clue.text: When to bring in second book

indicators.note: the word for when takes in the word for a second

parts.note: as means when, as in 'as I left'
a mo is a moment, a second

explanation.surface: Someone asks when they should bring in a second volume.
explanation.walkthrough: 'second book' reads as a sequel; 'second' is a moment, and the book is one of the Bible's.
explanation.definitionFit: This prophet's name is the title of a book of the Old Testament.

clue.text: One who changes places without being seen

definitions.text: One who changes places without being seen

parts.words: One who changes places without being seen
parts.note: a theatre hand moves the sets between scenes, out of the audience's sight

explanation.surface: Someone slips from spot to spot unnoticed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'places' means the settings on stage, and the work is done behind the curtain.
explanation.definitionFit: A stagehand who moves scenery in a theatre changes the stage settings out of view.

clue.text: Slightly drunk old Scots poet and reveller

parts.note: merry is a mild word for tipsy
maker (makar) is the old Scots word for a poet

explanation.surface: A tipsy old Scottish bard who loves a party.
explanation.walkthrough: In old Scots a poet is a makar or maker, one who makes verse.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who takes part in festivities is a reveller, a person enjoying lively celebration.

clue.text: Iolanthe's imperishable part

definitions.note: read as 'Iolanthe is': the title heroine of the Gilbert and Sullivan opera, one of a kind of fairy

indicators.note: part of imperishable means a run of its letters

explanation.surface: Iolanthe's role in the opera will never die.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Iolanthe's' is 'Iolanthe is', so the definition is the thing she is. 'part' signals letters 3-6 of 'imperishable'.
explanation.definitionFit: In Gilbert and Sullivan's opera the heroine is a fairy, the Persian sprite of this name.

clue.text: Where Irish may seen under lock and key

definitions.text: Where Irish may seen under lock and key

parts.words: Where Irish may seen under lock and key
parts.note: a lockable stand displaying decanters keeps Irish whiskey visible but out of reach

explanation.surface: Somewhere the Irish might be kept locked up.
explanation.walkthrough: As printed the clue lacks 'be' ('may be seen'). 'Irish' is Irish whiskey. The stand is named after the mythical king tortured by fruit and water just out of reach.
explanation.definitionFit: A Victorian decanter stand with a locking bar shows the spirits while keeping them unreachable.

clue.text: Someone seen by postman looking through a window?

definitions.text: Someone seen by postman looking through a window?

parts.words: Someone seen by postman looking through a window?
parts.note: a window envelope shows the recipient's name through its clear panel

explanation.surface: A postman spots someone peering out of a window.
explanation.walkthrough: The window is on the envelope, not the house.
explanation.definitionFit: The person to whom a letter is directed has their name visible through a window envelope.

clue.text: Woman swore, not being admitted

parts.note: Una is a woman's name
to swear is to vow

explanation.surface: A woman cursed after being refused entry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'swore' looks like cursing; here it is making a vow, and 'admitted' means confessed, not let in.
explanation.definitionFit: Something not openly acknowledged or confessed is unadmitted, which is this.

clue.text: Acting in charade

definitions.meaning: acting is make-believe, putting on a show
a charade is an absurd sham or pose

explanation.surface: Someone performs in a parlour game of mime.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are senses of a false show: play-acting, and a transparent sham kept up for appearances.

clue.text: Face exploratory discussion only half prepared

indicators.note: only half of the word is made ready, so take its first half

parts.note: a dialogue is an exchange of views to explore an issue

explanation.surface: Someone faces talks they have only half got ready for.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Face' looks like a verb; it is a clock face, and 'only half prepared' keeps DIAL from DIALOGUE.
explanation.definitionFit: The face of a clock or watch, marked with numbers, is its dial.

clue.text: Play some more before officer comes in

indicators.note: the officer arrives inside the word for before

parts.note: ere is a poetic word for before
NCO is a non-commissioned officer

explanation.surface: A band plays on before the officer arrives.
explanation.walkthrough: 'officer' here is the army's non-commissioned kind, a sergeant or corporal, not a commissioned one.
explanation.definitionFit: A repeated or extra performance at the audience's demand is this.

clue.text: Lacking foresight in island capital, on one motorway

indicators.note: the capital follows one and the motorway in the across entry

parts.note: the Roman numeral I is one
M, as in M1, is a British motorway
Providence is the capital of Rhode Island

explanation.surface: Someone shows no foresight on an island capital's motorway.
explanation.walkthrough: 'island capital' suggests somewhere like Valletta; it is Providence, capital of the US state Rhode Island.
explanation.definitionFit: Lack of foresight or thrift is improvidence; the noun here is the state of lacking it.

clue.text: Return to bank, putting in third of deposits

indicators.note: the letter is put inside the word for bank

parts.note: to bank on is to rely on

explanation.surface: A trip back to the bank to pay in deposits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bank' looks like a building; as a verb it means rely. P is third in 'deposits'.
explanation.definitionFit: A reply is a return, as in a witty retort or answer.

clue.text: Eat hurriedly in a bar

definitions.meaning: to ... food is to gulp it down
a sliding bar that fastens a door

explanation.surface: Someone wolfs a meal in a pub.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses: gobbling food fast, and the metal rod sliding into a socket to fasten a door.

clue.text: Captain and squadron leader taking nap

indicators.note: the leader of squadron is its opening letter

parts.note: kip is slang for a nap

explanation.surface: The captain and the squadron leader are having a snooze.
explanation.walkthrough: 'squadron leader' reads as an RAF rank, but gives the letter S.
explanation.definitionFit: Skip is short for skipper, the captain of a team or a boat.

clue.text: Just look at how some dummies are dressed!

definitions.text: Just look at how some dummies are dressed!

parts.words: Just look at how some dummies are dressed!
parts.note: shop mannequins are dressed in the display window, and browsers only gaze at them

explanation.surface: An exclamation at how badly some fools are dressed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dummies' are mannequins, not fools; the whole clue also means to browse without buying.
explanation.definitionFit: Browsing displays without buying is this; the clue's dummies are mannequins arranged in a store's front display.

clue.text: Became strained and anxious when first ignored in conversation

indicators.note: spoken in conversation the clipped word is heard

parts.note: anxious is afraid, and ignoring the first letter leaves fraid

explanation.surface: Someone grew tense and nervous when first snubbed in a chat.
explanation.walkthrough: AFRAID (anxious) loses its first letter, and the colloquial 'fraid sounds like the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Nerves or tempers that wore thin and became tense are said to have done this.

clue.text: Canines from particular force accompanying detective

parts.note: a private eye is a detective
teeth means the power to enforce, as in a law with teeth

explanation.surface: Police dogs from a special force go out with a detective.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Canines' suggests dogs; here it means the pointed teeth below the eyes. 'accompanying' sets the force beside the detective.
explanation.definitionFit: The canine teeth of the upper jaw are called this, lying directly under the eyes.
